                                                       Abstract
            We give simple deterministic reductions demonstrating the NP-hardness of approximating
        the nearest codeword problem and minimum distance problem within arbitrary constant factors
        (and almost-polynomial factors assuming NP cannot be solved in quasipolynomial time). The
        starting point is a simple NP-hardness result without a gap, and is thus “PCP-free.” Our
        approach is inspired by that of Bhattiprolu and Lee [BL24] who give a PCP-free randomized
        reduction for similar problems over the integers and the reals. We leverage the existence of
        ε-balanced codes to derandomize and further simplify their reduction for the case of finite fields.


1       Introduction
    Error-correcting codes are fundamental mathematical objects with many applications across
computing. A long line of work has been studying the complexity of basic computational problems
on codes, especially the Nearest Codeword Problem (NCP) and the Minimum Distance Problem
(MDP) [BMvT78, ABSS97, Var97, DMS03, CW12, AK14, Mic14] defined below.

Definition 1 (Nearest Codeword Problem (NCP)1 ).
An instance of NCP over a finite field Fq consists of an affine subspace V ⊆ Fnq , where V is encoded
using any basis. The goal is to find the minimum Hamming weight of any vector x ∈ V .

MDP is a homogeneous variant of NCP:

Definition 2 (Minimum Distance Problem (MDP)).
An instance of MDP over a finite field Fq consists of a subspace V ⊆ Fnq . The goal is to find the
minimum Hamming weight of any nonzero vector x ∈ V .

Our Results. We give a new elementary proof of the inapproximability of these problems, avoiding
the PCP theorem. It has traditionally been much easier to show hardness for the non-homogeneous
variant NCP compared to the homogeneous version MDP. Previous approaches first establish inap-
proximability of NCP as a quick corollary of the PCP theorem, and then employ non-trivial coding

Related Work. Proving NP-Hardness of exactly computing MDP was a question posed in
[BMvT78], and was resolved in the affirmative by Vardy [Var97], using as a gadget a Reed-
Solomon code concatenated with the Hadamard code. The analog for MDP for point lattices,
the Shortest Vector Problem (SVP), was shown to be NP-hard under randomized reductions by
Ajtai [Ajt98].2 Micciancio [Mic01] then established hardness of approximating SVP within a con-
stant factor bounded away from 1 via a reduction from the affine version, the Closest Vector Prob-
lem (CVP), using “locally dense” lattices as key gadgets. Dumer, Micciancio and Sudan [DMS03]
adapted the locally dense gadgets framework to the setting of linear codes and established constant-
factor inapproximability of MDP over any finite field, under randomized reductions (the inapprox-
imability factor can be amplified to any desired constant via tensoring). A locally dense code is
a code of minimum distance d, that admits a Hamming ball of smaller radius ((1 − ε)d for some
constant ε > 0) containing exponentially many codewords.
     Cheng and Wan [CW12] derandomized the proof of [DMS03] by giving a deterministic con-
struction of a locally dense gadget over any finite field. In particular they give an explicit Hamming
ball of radius 0.67d that contains exponentially many codewords of an explicit code of distance d.
The proof of Cheng and Wan’s result is fairly deep, making use of Weil’s character sum estimate.
      Austrin and Khot [AK14] gave a simpler proof of deterministic hardness of MDP by mak-
ing use of tensor codes. Building on this, Micciancio [Mic14] proved that for the special case of
F2 , the tensoring of any base code with large distance yields a significantly simpler deterministic
construction of a locally dense gadget than the proof of [CW12].
     More recently, Bhattiprolu and Lee [BL24] observed that if the base code C being tensored has
a weak version of the local density property (i.e. there is a Hamming ball of radius (1+ε)d containing
exponentially many codewords in C) and an additional property that linearly independent minimal
weight codewords do not overlap much in support (which always holds over finite fields), then
the reduction in [AK14] can be simplified (in particular bypassing the PCP theorem) as well as
generalized to larger fields (including the reals). However, [BL24] uses a random base code, and
therefore the reduction is randomized.
    In this work, we derandomize (and further simplify) the reduction in [BL24] for the special
case of finite fields. We show that the tensoring of any ε-balanced code (all of whose nonzero
codewords have Hamming weights within a (1 ± ε) factor of each other) can be used to give a

choose the base code to be a low rate Reed-Solomon code concatenated with a Hadamard code
(which is ε-balanced). This gives a new deterministic proof of the hardness of MDP, that is simpler
than [AK14] in two ways; first the PCP theorem is not used, and secondly, the proof of the code
construction is elementary whereas in [AK14] the proof (for fields of size ≥ 3) uses Viola’s [Vio09]
construction of a pseudorandom generator for low degree polynomials.
      A recent work [BHI+ 24] also achieves constant inapproximability of NCP without using the
PCP theorem (using multiplication codes). They even manage at most constant factor blow-up on
the parameters when reducing from 3SAT, which leads to an exponential runtime lower bound for
NCP (under the Exponential Time Hypothesis). Our reduction is nevertheless interesting due to
its simplicity and also since it works essentially verbatim for MDP.

     To prove APX-hardness of MDP, we start with the NP-hardness of determining whether a
system of homogeneous quadratic equations is satisfiable:
Proposition 5 (Homogeneous Quadratic Equations Hardness).
Fix any finite field Fq . Given n variables x1 , . . . , xn and m quadratic equations
Q1 (xxT ) = 0, . . . , Qm (xxT ) = 0, it is NP-hard to distinguish between the following two cases:

    • (YES) There exists a non-zero vector x ∈ {0, 1}n satisfying all m equations.
    • (NO) There is no non-zero x ∈ Fnq satisfying all m equations.

Furthermore, the hardness holds with the distinguished-coordinate property, i.e., in the YES case,
there is a non-zero vector x satisfying all equations as well as xn = 1.

     Note that above the completeness guarantees a solution x ∈ {0, 1}n whereas the soundness
rules out x ∈ Fnq —the above is thus a promise problem. Proposition 5 is proved via reduction
from the circuit satisfiability (Circuit-SAT) problem. The proof follows the standard template
for exact NP-Hardness results, and we defer it to Appendix A.

3    Rank testing via tensor codes
        The gap-producing randomized reduction in [BL24] proceeds by first observing that testing
(nonzero) satisfiability of a system of quadratic equations Q1 (xxT ) = 0, . . . , Qm (xxT ) = 0 is equiv-
alent to testing whether or not the subspace of matrices given by {X : X = X T , Q1 (X) =
0, . . . , Qm (X) = 0} contains a rank-1 matrix. Then [BL24] shows how tensoring of a base code
with appropriate structure can be used to test via Hamming weight if a matrix subspace contains a
rank-1 matrix. We follow the same template, but our approach is even simpler as over finite fields,
we are able to embed the above subspace directly inside a tensor code. We begin by discussing the
simple but crucial properties of the Hamming weight of matrices of rank > 1 in a tensor code.

Hamming Weight of Rank ≥ 2 Elements of a Tensor Code. Recall that in Observation 6,
the upper bound ∥U ∥20 on ∥U ⊗ U ∥0 (taking V = U ) is attained by a rank-1 matrix. Implicit
in [AK14] is the insightful observation that codewords of rank ≥ 2 in U ⊗ U have Hamming weight
at least (1 + 1q )∥U ∥20 (over a finite field Fq ), which is significantly larger than the minimum distance.
We include the proof here for completeness.

Lemma 8. For any subspace U ⊂ Fnq and any M ∈ U ⊗ U of rank at least 2, we have ∥M ∥0 ≥
(1 + 1q ) · ∥U ∥20 .

Proof. Since M is of rank at least two, there are two linearly independent columns, that by Fact 9
(proved below), have joint support of size at least (1 + 1q )d. Thus at least (1 + 1q )d rows of M are
non-zero, and since they lie inside U , each of these rows has at least ∥U ∥0 non-zero entries. Thus
∥M ∥0 ≥ (1 + 1q )∥U ∥20 .

ε-Balanced Codes. At the heart of our reduction that generates constant factor hardness for
MDP is the observation that the above connection between rank and Hamming weight can be made
two-sided, assuming the base code being tensored is ε-balanced. More specifically, we observe that
any codeword in C ⊗ C for an ε-balanced code C has near-minimum Hamming weight if and only
if it is rank-1.

5    Inapproximability of NCP
    In this section we will prove Theorem 4 using a straightforward gap-preserving reduction from
MDP. Towards this end, we fist note that the MDP reduction shown above can be easily modified
to have the distinguished-coordinate property. We defer the proof to the appendix.

Proposition 13 (MDP Hardness with a Distinguished Coordinate).
For any finite field Fq and any constant c > 1 (resp. for any constant ε > 0), it is NP-hard (resp.
Quasi-NP-Hard) given an input subspace V ⊆ FN   q to distinguish between the following cases:

    • (YES) There exists x ∈ V \ {0} satisfying ∥x∥0 ≤ k, xN = 1;

    • (NO) For all x ∈ V \ {0}, ∥x∥0 > c · k (resp. ∥x∥0 > 2log         N · k).


Proof of Theorem 4. Consider the reduction from MDP (with a distinguished coordinate) to NCP,
given by mapping a subspace V ⊆ Fnq to the affine subspace V ′ := {x ∈ V : xn = 1}. The claim
then follows from Proposition 13.
     Completeness follows from the distinguished-coordinate property of MDP.
     For soundness, note that any x ∈ V ′ is a non-zero vector in V , with the same sparsity.

Remark 14. A gap-preserving Cook-reduction from MDP to NCP was known in the literature (see
e.g., [GMSS99] and Exercise 23.13 in [GRS18]). However, we have a Karp-reduction here thanks
to the distinguished-coordinate property.
    We also remark that there are non-trivial ways to amplify gap for NCP (see e.g., Theorem
22 of [LLL24] and Section 4.2 of [BGKM18]). Thus one can start with the NP-hardness of non-
homogeneous quadratic equations, perform the reduction in Section 4 to get a mild constant gap for
NCP, and then amplify the gap. This is another way to prove Theorem 4.

Remark 15. The relatively near codeword problem parameterized by ρ ∈ (0, ∞) (denoted by
RNC (ρ) ) is a promise problem defined as follows. Given a subspace V ⊆ Fnq of an (unknown)
minimum distance d, a vector b ∈ Fnq and an integer t with the promise that t < ρ · d, the task is to
find a codeword in V of hamming distance at most t from b.
    Our reduction for NCP yields NP-Hardness of RNC (1+ε) for any fixed ε > 0 (it also yields
hardness for the gap version of RNC for an appropriately small constant gap). [DMS03] show
hardness of RNC (ρ) for any ρ > 1/2, albeit under randomized reductions.
